cards.body: On October 11, NASA's Perseverance rover passed 45.22 km (28.1 miles) of total driving on Mars, a record recognized by Guinness. Engineers got there by letting it tilt more steeply and navigate itself by matching ground photos to orbital maps.
cards.more:
The rover had been about 200 m short earlier but stopped to study rocks before claiming the record.
One upgrade lets it work out where it is by comparing its own camera images with pictures taken from orbit, so it needs less help from Earth.
The extra computer it uses for this needed software protection against radiation flipping bits in memory. NASA says it is also exploring generative AI for route planning, but that is not in use yet.
cards.title: Perseverance has now driven farther than any vehicle on another world

cards.body: Deep-sleep slow waves normally sweep across the brain together. A Berkeley team found that older adults with more tau protein in the frontal cortex had shorter, more isolated waves, and they recalled fewer word pairs the next morning.
cards.more:
The study, in Nature Neuroscience, combined sleep EEG with PET brain scans and compared young adults with people in their mid-60s to mid-70s.
In people followed for several years, rising tau came with less coordinated waves and worse overnight memory.
The authors stress this is a correlation: it does not prove tau causes the memory loss or that the waves are the mechanism. Some participants with tau were cognitively normal for their age.
cards.title: 'Lonely' sleep waves track tau buildup and weaker overnight memory

cards.body: Nottingham researchers made a fluoride-free protein gel that seeps into enamel microcracks and uses calcium and phosphate from saliva to grow new, aligned crystals. In lab tests mimicking brushing and acidic food, the new layer behaved much like healthy enamel.
cards.more:
Enamel normally cannot repair itself because the cells that make it are gone once a tooth erupts. The gel mimics the proteins that guide enamel growth in childhood.
It also formed an enamel-like coat over exposed dentine, the softer layer underneath.
These are lab results only; long-term performance in real mouths is untested. A spin-out company is developing it and hopes for a first product soon.
cards.title: A lab-made gel coaxed tooth enamel to regrow in the lab

cards.body: An international guideline in Nature Medicine sets out more than 60 recommendations for phage therapy: using viruses that infect bacteria to treat drug-resistant infections. It covers picking, testing, making and giving the phages, but does not endorse routine use.
cards.more:
It was drafted by 20 professional bodies, 18 experts including regulators, and two patient groups, led by German infectious-disease specialists.
In one Belgian series of 100 patients, 77% improved and the target bacteria became undetectable in 61%. That series had no control group, so it cannot show the phages caused the recovery.
Controlled trials are still needed to show how reliably the treatment works.
cards.title: Doctors now have a rulebook for treating superbugs with viruses

cards.body: Stanford's Peptide Predictor narrowed about 20,000 human genes to 373 hormone precursors and flagged a tiny 12-amino-acid peptide called BRP. In mice and minipigs, one dose cut food intake by up to half over the next hour.
cards.more:
In obese mice dosed daily for 14 days, treated animals lost about 3 g, mostly fat, while untreated ones gained about 3 g.
In lab-grown neurons, BRP boosted activity about tenfold, compared with threefold for GLP-1, the hormone that drugs like Ozempic mimic.
This is animal work only. Human safety, side effects like nausea, and even which receptor BRP acts on are still unknown. The lead scientist co-founded a company developing it.
cards.title: An algorithm sifted 20,000 genes and found an appetite-cutting peptide

cards.body: MIT chemists joined nanoparticles with flexible polymer strands tipped with opposite charges, instead of the usual rigid links. Changing particle size and strand length produced open, previously unseen crystal arrangements of particles.
cards.more:
For about two decades, nanoparticle crystals were mostly built with stiff connectors, which limits how particles can pack.
With flexible linkers, how many neighbours each particle bonds to depends on charge and flexibility, opening new geometries.
The team, publishing in Nature Materials, says uses in optics, catalysis and energy are possible but need more development.
cards.title: Floppy, charged links built never-before-seen nanoparticle crystals

cards.body: Physicists in Brazil and China propose reading a superconducting qubit by measuring the tiny current it drives around a superconducting loop, sensed by a nearby SQUID. In noisy simulations, readout accuracy reached up to 99.85%.
cards.more:
Reading a qubit usually means coupling it to extra helper qubits, which adds complexity and errors.
Here the current oscillates with no applied voltage, and its offset, size and timing encode the qubit's state.
The work, in Physical Review B, is purely theoretical. The device geometry has not been built yet.
cards.title: A proposed way to read a qubit by listening to its supercurrent

cards.body: A Texas A&M analysis pooled 50,000 correlations from 137 test batteries. Picking out the sounds inside words and knowing vocabulary and background facts were the most reliable predictors of reading ability; visual processing showed no meaningful link.
cards.more:
General intelligence was linked to reading, but less strongly than some earlier reviews suggested. Memory, reasoning and processing speed played supporting roles.
This is a synthesis of correlations, so it shows what goes together, not what causes reading success.
The paper appeared in the Journal of Intelligence.
cards.title: Hearing sounds in words and knowing words predict reading best

cards.body: Metal-organic frameworks are sponge-like crystals that can be melted into glass. German and UK chemists added a molecule called phenanthroline before melting; it lowered the melting point and bonded to the metal atoms, rewiring the glass's structure.
cards.more:
The amount added controls how much the structure changes, giving a dial for tuning the material.
Gentler melting also avoided unwanted breakdown products in cobalt-based glasses.
The study is in Nature Materials. Uses in catalysts, sensors, batteries and gas storage are possibilities, not demonstrations.
cards.title: A helper molecule lets chemists reshape a new kind of glass

cards.body: Residents in a Baton Rouge neighbourhood say Amazon's delivery drones have buzzed overhead almost nonstop since September; one counted a drone every 48 seconds. As drone firms plan huge expansions, towns and states are pushing back.
cards.more:
The drones fly from a site about 3 km away. An FAA environmental review allows up to 1,000 deliveries a day there.
Amazon aims to serve 500 municipalities by end of 2026, and other firms plan hundreds of hubs. In September, 15 states sued the FAA over easing environmental review.
Who controls the low airspace over private homes is still legally unsettled.
cards.title: Delivery drones are bringing a new noise complaint to US suburbs

cards.body: French archaeologists excavated a Neolithic cemetery at Champigny-sur-Marne with 11 graves and 30 megaliths. Its centrepiece is a toppled, human-shaped menhir weighing over 9 tonnes that once stood more than 3 m tall, possibly painted.
cards.more:
The stone has a carved belt, an arc of small cup-shaped hollows, and faint white and black stains that may be pigment.
Most graves had a post hole near the head. One held an adult buried seated, legs encased in mineral deposits.
The dig was run by Inrap, France's preventive archaeology institute.
cards.title: A 6,500-year-old human-shaped standing stone found near Paris

cards.body: A brass combination lock recovered off Wales was scanned with micro-CT, revealing its hidden mechanism. A Cardiff University researcher matched the notches to letters and found the four-letter code: ANCE.
cards.more:
The wreck is thought to be the Ann Frances, an English merchant ship lost in a storm in 1583.
The lock lay near Spanish silver coins and probably secured a small chest of valuables that has not survived.
The ship's identity and the chest's contents are interpretations, and the work has not yet appeared in a journal.
cards.title: X-ray scans cracked the code of a lock from a 1583 shipwreck

cards.body: On November 5 the Bank of England lifted its key rate from 3.75% to 4%. Eight of nine policymakers voted for the move, and the one dissenter wanted a bigger hike. Governor Andrew Bailey said more rises may follow if energy prices stay high.
cards.more:
Markets had not fully expected a split in favour of a larger rise.
Two-year UK government bond yields edged up after the decision, and traders priced in more tightening by the end of 2027.
Raising rates makes borrowing dearer, which cools spending and, over time, inflation.
cards.title: The Bank of England raised rates for the first time in three years

cards.body: Most come from the Sun's core and pass straight through you, and the whole Earth, almost never touching an atom. IceCube in Antarctica uses a cubic kilometre of ice to catch a few dozen of the most energetic ones a year.
cards.more:
Some of IceCube's catches carry around 10 billion times the energy of a typical solar neutrino; where they come from is still unknown.
The detector watches for faint blue flashes when a rare neutrino does hit something in the ice.

stat.label: neutrinos through each square centimetre of you, every second

cards.title: Neutrinos are pouring through you right now

cards.body: US stocks slid on November 5 as investors dumped AI and semiconductor shares. The Nasdaq fell into a correction, meaning 10% below its recent high. Here are the one-day drops.
cards.more:
The Dow lost about 1,833 points. Nvidia, Micron and AMD were among the big decliners.
Wall Street's fear gauge, the VIX, jumped by about 70%.
cards.title: Chip stocks fell hardest in Thursday's sell-off

beats: Bacteriophages, or phages, are viruses that infect only bacteria, never human cells.
A phage lands on a bacterium, latches onto a specific surface molecule, and injects its DNA.
That DNA hijacks the cell's machinery to build dozens of new phages inside it.
The phages then burst the cell open and go hunting for the next bacterium.
Each phage targets a narrow range of strains, so doctors must match the phage to the infection.
cards.more:
Phages were discovered over a century ago, around 1915 to 1917, but antibiotics overshadowed them in the West.
Rising antibiotic resistance has revived interest, especially for infections nothing else can treat.
cards.title: How a virus can kill bacteria for us

beats: A correction is a fall of at least 10% from a recent peak.
A bear market is a deeper fall, usually 20% or more from the peak.
The thresholds are conventions, not laws; nothing special happens at exactly 10%.
Corrections are fairly common and many recover within months, though some deepen.
The labels describe the past move; they do not predict what comes next.
cards.title: What 'correction' and 'bear market' actually mean

beats: Normally, trade winds push warm surface water west across the tropical Pacific toward Asia.
In an El Niño, those winds weaken and the warm water sloshes back east toward South America.
Warm water feeds rising air and storms, so rainfall patterns shift with it.
Those shifts ripple through the atmosphere, bringing droughts to some regions and floods to others.
Because the ocean also releases heat, El Niño years tend to push global temperatures up.
cards.title: How El Niño reshuffles the world's weather

beats: Suppose someone claims to have a complete list of all prime numbers.
Multiply every prime on the list together, then add one.
Dividing that number by any listed prime always leaves a remainder of one.
So its prime factors must be missing from the list.
No list can be complete; Euclid proved this about 2,300 years ago.
cards.title: Why the primes never run out

beats: Lab experiments are slow and costly, so you cannot test every candidate molecule.
A model learns patterns from known examples, such as what real hormones look like.
It scores thousands of untested candidates by how closely they fit those patterns.
Scientists then test only the top few in the lab.
The AI suggests; the experiments decide whether the suggestion was right.
cards.title: How AI narrows a haystack before scientists search it

beats: Spoken words are built from small sound units called phonemes, like the c-a-t in 'cat'.
Children first learn to hear and juggle these sounds, often through rhymes and word games.
Reading means linking letters to those sounds and blending them into words.
A child who can't hear the separate sounds has nothing for the letters to attach to.
Vocabulary then turns the decoded word into meaning, which is why both skills matter.
cards.title: Why hearing sounds inside words unlocks reading

beats: A SQUID is a loop of superconducting wire broken by one or two ultra-thin barriers.
In a superconducting loop, magnetic flux comes only in fixed, tiny steps.
The current through the barriers swings sharply as the field changes by a fraction of a step.
That makes SQUIDs among the most sensitive magnetic field detectors ever built.
Hospitals use them to map the faint magnetic fields of brain activity, called MEG.
cards.title: What a SQUID is, and why it can sense your brainwaves

myth.claim: Eating sugar makes children hyper and hard to control.
myth.truth: Double-blind trials, where nobody knew who got sugar, found no effect on behaviour. Parents who merely believed their child had sugar rated them as more hyperactive. Exciting settings like parties likely explain the rest.

cards.title: Sugar makes kids hyperactive

myth.claim: Astronauts float because there's no gravity in orbit.
myth.truth: At the station's height, gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they and the station are falling together around Earth, moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it.

cards.title: There's no gravity on the space station

myth.truth: He was about 1.69 m (5 ft 7 in), average or a bit above for a Frenchman of his time. Confusion between French and English inches, British cartoons, and his nickname 'the little corporal' built the legend.

cards.title: Napoleon was tiny

quiz.q: Which gas makes up the largest share of Earth's atmosphere?
quiz.why: Nitrogen is about 78% of dry air; oxygen is about 21%, argon nearly 1%, and CO2 only about 0.04%.

cards.title: What is most of the air you breathe?

quiz.why: One third is 0.333..., and three thirds is 0.999..., which is 1. No number fits between them, so they are the same.

cards.title: Is 0.999... really equal to 1?

quiz.q: 'Clue' grew out of an old word for what?
quiz.why: A 'clew' was a ball of yarn. In the Greek myth, Theseus unwound one to find his way out of the labyrinth, so a clue became anything that guides you to an answer.

cards.title: Where does the word 'clue' come from?

cards.body: Hubble has no engine, and air drag is slowly lowering its orbit; NASA expects reentry around 2033 to 2034. On October 29 the agency asked industry for ideas: boost it higher, service it, or retire it safely. A boost would need to happen by 2032.
cards.more:
The request for information is open until November 30. It is a survey of what technology exists, not an approved mission.
The three options on the table are a spacecraft that pushes Hubble to a higher orbit, a servicing mission to upgrade it, or a controlled descent into the atmosphere or disposal in orbit.
Hubble is run from NASA Goddard, with science operations at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore and ESA as a partner.
cards.title: NASA is asking companies how to rescue Hubble before it falls

cards.body: ESA's Hera spacecraft photographed Didymos and its small moon Dimorphos as two separate objects on October 18, from about 1,280 km away. NASA's DART probe slammed into Dimorphos in 2022. Hera will now study the crash site, with its first detailed images due on November 25.
cards.more:
Dimorphos is about 151 metres across and circles Didymos, which is about 780 metres wide, at a distance of roughly 1.15 km.
DART's 2022 impact shortened that orbit by about 33 minutes, more than simulations predicted. Nobody yet knows whether it left a crater or reshaped the whole asteroid.
Hera slowed to 20 metres per second relative to the pair after two thruster burns in early October. It will release two shoebox-sized CubeSats to help measure mass and internal structure.
cards.title: Hera has the asteroid pair that DART hit in its sights

cards.body: Radio images from 2021 to 2026 show Betelgeuse looking more stretched when a suspected companion star, Siwarha, is farthest to one side, and rounder when it passes in front or behind. Astronomers call it strong evidence the companion disturbs the giant's outer layers, though more observations are needed.
cards.more:
Siwarha was first proposed in 2024 to explain a roughly 2,100-day brightness cycle. It is too faint to see directly at radio wavelengths.
The team, led by Lynn Matthews of MIT Haystack Observatory, used the VLA and ALMA telescopes at seven frequencies. They also mapped a cool layer in the star's atmosphere at about 2,200 kelvin.
The work appears in The Astronomical Journal.
cards.title: A hidden companion may be stirring Betelgeuse's atmosphere

cards.body: A SLAC-led team fired circularly polarised X-rays at manganese telluride, long filed as an ordinary antiferromagnet. They measured a 'handed' signal that only an altermagnet should produce. Altermagnets have no overall magnetic pull, yet can steer electron spins, which could help future memory chips.
cards.more:
For decades, magnets came in two families: ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. The name altermagnet was only coined in 2022.
The team ran the experiment at the European Synchrotron in France in 2024 and reproduced it in early 2025. The paper is in Science.
Useful devices are still a long way off. The next step is learning to control these magnetic states with light and electricity.
cards.title: X-rays caught a third kind of magnetism in action

cards.body: Quark-gluon plasma, the matter that filled the universe in its first millionths of a second, was thought to need heavy nuclei like lead. All four big LHC experiments now report signs of it in collisions of much lighter oxygen and neon nuclei. Several results are still preliminary.
cards.more:
The plasma forms at more than 100,000 times the temperature at the Sun's core. Quarks and gluons, normally locked inside protons and neutrons, flow freely.
The main clue is that fast particles lose energy crossing the fireball, so fewer emerge than in proton collisions. Physicists note that a drop in particles alone doesn't prove energy loss.
The findings come a year after the LHC's first-ever oxygen collisions.
cards.title: Even small atoms can make the Big Bang's hot soup

cards.body: In a 2025 Anthropic experiment, researchers injected a concept's activity pattern into a language model; the most capable version flagged the intrusion in about 20% of trials. Other researchers found simpler explanations for naming the concept, but the detection itself has held up. Whether that counts as introspection is hotly debated.
cards.more:
Control copies of the model, with nothing injected, never reported an injection.
Kyle Mahowald and Harvey Lederman showed that naming the planted concept and detecting that something was planted are separate skills; they could break one without the other. Models often guessed the wrong concept.
No one involved claims this shows the models have experiences. The question is whether 'noticing an anomaly' is a weak form of self-knowledge or just pattern matching.
cards.title: Can an AI notice a thought planted in its own network?

cards.body: Agility Robotics says its new Digit 5 lifts 23-kilogram bins onto 1.75-metre shelves and runs 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge. When a person approaches, it sets down its load, sits on the floor and cuts motor power. These are the company's own claims, written by its co-founder.
cards.more:
Jonathan Hurst, who co-founded Agility in 2015, says the safety behaviour took two years to build. The robot weighs over 120 kg, so falling on someone is a real risk.
It is designed to work 20 hours a day. The battery and cooling take up about three quarters of the torso.
The company says its Oregon factory can make more than 10,000 per year.
cards.title: A warehouse humanoid that sits down when people get close

cards.body: A University of Washington study estimates that year-round daylight saving time would add over a billion US school trips made before sunrise. In traffic records, fatal crashes involving school-age pedestrians were about twice as likely on dark mornings as after sunrise. That is an association, not proof of cause.
cards.more:
The team analysed 14 of the 19 US states that have approved permanent daylight saving measures. Georgia saw the largest jump, about 71 million extra dark commutes.
The nationwide estimate assumes students leave home around 8 a.m., so the authors think it is probably too low; the press release puts it at 2 billion or more.
The paper appears in Current Biology. The authors also warn that darker mornings could cancel out the sleep gains of later school start times.
cards.title: Permanent daylight saving time would put more kids on dark roads

cards.body: McGill and Toronto researchers watched hundreds of hippocampus neurons in mice that learned one place meant danger and another meant safety. After fear learning, the brain's patterns for the two places started to overlap. That may speed up threat recall at the cost of precision. Human links remain unproven.
cards.more:
The mice wore miniature microscopes and were 'teleported' between virtual environments using augmented reality.
The authors suggest this kind of overlap might help explain why fear spreads to safe situations in anxiety and PTSD, but they stress more research is needed.
The study appears in Nature Neuroscience.
cards.title: Fear may blur the brain's line between danger and safety

cards.body: A new hypothesis traces the brain's crossed wiring back to jawless fish in the Cambrian, more than 500 million years ago. Their crossed visual pathways may have set a template, and later senses and movement circuits were built on top of it. It's an idea, not a new experiment.
cards.more:
Every living vertebrate has an optic chiasm, where visual nerves cross, and an optic tectum, a visual processing hub. The authors argue other pathways followed that layout.
The crossing didn't have to be an advantage; it may simply have been inherited and built upon.
Martin Wessendorf and Daniel Wang published the idea in Frontiers in Neuroanatomy. They suggest fossil skulls of jawless fish might help test it.
cards.title: Why your left brain moves your right hand: a 500-million-year answer

cards.body: Visitors and guides walked past them for decades, but Cova de la Font Major in Catalonia holds 280 engraved motifs at least 19,000 years old, including 55 animals. They were nearly invisible under headlamps, which light the walls head-on. The findings are published in Antiquity.
cards.more:
Archaeologist Josep Maria Vergès first spotted vertical lines in 2019 and studied the gallery with Míriam Salas-Altès of IPHES-CERCA.
The animals include horses, deer and wild cattle, plus an unusual bear drawn with its ears facing forward. Few sites in the region have more than 20 animal figures.
The gallery stays closed to the public because its walls are fragile, and sediment still blocks other passages.
cards.title: 280 Ice Age engravings hid in a Spanish tourist cave

cards.body: DNA from a woman who lived about 30,000 years ago in Isturitz Cave, France, is the oldest genome-wide data yet from a modern human in southwestern Europe. It suggests eastern and western Ice Age groups mixed around 32,000 years ago. Iberia later served as a refuge in the coldest times.
cards.more:
The work, led by the University of Vienna, appears in Science Advances. It covers the Gravettian culture, roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago.
At El Mirón Cave in Spain, the team recovered human DNA straight from 22,000-year-old sediment, with no bones or teeth.
The mixing date comes from genetic modelling, so it is an estimate.
cards.title: A 30,000-year-old genome shows Ice Age Europe was well connected

cards.body: Ohio State researchers dated ice from the Guliya ice cap using rare radioactive forms of beryllium and chlorine. The bottom layers may be more than 128,000 years old, over 100,000 years older than earlier estimates. That would make Guliya a rare long climate record from outside the poles.
cards.more:
The cores were drilled in 1992 and 2015. Earlier work suggested they reached back only to the middle of the current warm period, a few thousand years ago.
The team cross-checked its dates against oxygen isotope records in nearby cave deposits.
The paper, led by Lonnie Thompson, is in Science Advances. The researchers plan to study more samples.
cards.title: Tibetan glacier ice may be more than 128,000 years old

cards.body: A model tuned with two decades of observations projects that Antarctica's Thwaites Glacier could add up to 30 millimetres to global sea level by 2100, double earlier estimates. The model reproduced recent changes that standard models underestimated about fourfold. It is a projection, not a certainty.
cards.more:
The key is the grounding zone, where the glacier lifts off the seabed and starts to float. Radar satellites showed it shifting across several kilometres.
In one scenario the authors give a 60% chance that Thwaites detaches from a seabed ridge that now holds it back before 2100.
The study, from UC Irvine and NASA JPL, is in Nature Communications.
cards.title: Thwaites Glacier could add twice the sea-level rise once expected

cards.body: US imports rose 1.2% to a record $426.6 billion in September, but exports rose faster, so the trade deficit narrowed slightly to $105.0 billion. Economists had expected $108 billion. Imports of capital goods, such as computers and chips, also set a record.
cards.more:
Exports climbed 1.9% to $321.5 billion. Services exports hit an all-time high of $110.5 billion.
Because imports are subtracted when GDP is calculated, the import surge took 2.64 percentage points off third-quarter growth. The economy still grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the advance estimate.
The figures come from the Commerce Department, as reported by Reuters.
cards.title: US imports hit a record in September

beats: Every electron is a tiny magnet, called its spin, pointing up or down.
In a ferromagnet like iron, neighbouring spins line up, so their pulls add into one you can feel.
In an antiferromagnet, neighbours point opposite ways and cancel, so there's no outside pull.
Altermagnets also cancel overall, but the atoms around each spin are rotated, which breaks the symmetry.
That lets them sort moving electrons by spin like a ferromagnet, without stray fields that disturb nearby parts.
cards.more:
Ferromagnets store data in today's hard drives, but their stray fields limit how tightly bits can be packed.
Antiferromagnets are stable and fast, but hard to read because they cancel out. Altermagnets promise the best of both.
Manganese telluride is one of the first materials to show the effect clearly.
cards.title: The three families of magnets

beats: You don't need to blow up a dangerous asteroid; you just need it to arrive slightly early or late.
A small spacecraft crashing at high speed changes the asteroid's velocity by a tiny amount.
Debris blasted off the surface acts like a rocket exhaust, adding an extra shove.
Over years of orbiting, that tiny change grows into a miss of thousands of kilometres.
So the key is warning time: the earlier you nudge, the smaller the nudge can be.
cards.more:
NASA's DART tested this in 2022 on Dimorphos, a small moon of the asteroid Didymos, hitting at about 6.1 km/s.
It shortened Dimorphos's orbit by about 33 minutes, more than many models predicted, likely helped by the debris recoil.
ESA's Hera mission is now arriving to measure the asteroid's mass and the crater, if there is one, so future deflections can be planned precisely.
cards.title: How to move an asteroid by hitting it

beats: Each year's snow piles on the last and is squeezed into ice, layer by layer.
Tiny bubbles trap samples of the air from when the snow fell.
The ratio of heavy to light oxygen in the ice tracks how cold it was.
Deep down, layers get squashed too thin to count, so scientists date them by radioactive decay instead.
Read top to bottom, a core is a timeline of temperature, dust, volcanoes and greenhouse gases.
cards.more:
The longest polar ice cores, from Antarctica, reach back roughly 800,000 years or more.
Mountain glaciers, like Tibet's Guliya ice cap, are rarer archives because they usually melt and flow faster. They record climate where many people actually live.
Some glaciers are disappearing so quickly that scientists race to drill and store their cores before the record melts away.
cards.title: How an ice core remembers ancient climate

beats: A radioactive atom decays at a random moment, but huge groups behave very predictably.
A half-life is the time it takes for half of the atoms in a sample to decay.
After two half-lives a quarter remains; after ten, about one thousandth.
Measure how much is left compared with its decay products, and you can read off the age.
Carbon-14 dates bones up to about 50,000 years; slower isotopes like beryllium-10 date far older ice and rock.
cards.more:
This is exponential decay: the amount left shrinks by the same fraction in each equal stretch of time, no matter how much you start with.
Carbon-14's half-life is about 5,730 years. After roughly nine half-lives there is too little left to measure reliably.
The same maths describes drug levels in the blood and how quickly a hot drink cools toward room temperature.
cards.title: Half-life: the clock inside radioactive atoms

beats: A trade deficit means a country buys more goods and services from abroad than it sells.
It isn't a bill that comes due; buyers paid for each import when they bought it.
The dollars sent abroad often come back as foreign investment in shares, bonds or factories.
Deficits can widen when an economy is booming, because people and firms can afford more imports.
Whether a deficit is a problem depends on why it exists, not just on how big it is.
cards.more:
Economists track it because it's connected to saving and investment: a country that invests more than it saves must draw in money from abroad.
In GDP accounting, imports are subtracted, so an import surge can make growth look weaker even when spending is strong.
The US has run a trade deficit almost every year since the mid-1970s.
cards.title: What a trade deficit really means

beats: In the 1400s, English spelling was still loose, with words often spelled several ways.
The printing press, arriving in England in 1476, began freezing spellings in place.
Meanwhile, the Great Vowel Shift was changing how long vowels sounded, so speech drifted away from print.
Letters once spoken went silent, like the k in 'knight' and the gh in 'night'.
Some scholars even added letters to echo Latin, which is why 'debt' has a silent b.
cards.more:
The Great Vowel Shift ran roughly from 1400 to 1700. Before it, 'bite' sounded more like 'beet' and 'house' more like 'hoose'.
Early printers were often Flemish, and some spellings, like the h in 'ghost', show their influence.
Noah Webster's 1800s reforms, such as 'color' for 'colour', are why American and British spellings differ.
cards.title: Why English spelling is such a mess

myth.claim: Humans have five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch.
myth.truth: The five-sense list goes back to Aristotle. We also sense balance, the position of our limbs, temperature, pain and internal signals like hunger. Depending on how you count, scientists list anywhere from about nine to more than twenty.

cards.title: We have exactly five senses

myth.claim: Leaving a phone plugged in all night overcharges and ruins its battery.
myth.truth: Phones stop charging when full, and many hold at about 80% until shortly before you wake. What wears lithium-ion batteries most is heat and long stretches at very high or very low charge, so avoid charging under a pillow.

cards.title: Charging your phone overnight wrecks the battery

myth.claim: Before Columbus, most Europeans believed the Earth was flat.
myth.truth: Educated people had known the Earth was round since ancient Greece; Eratosthenes estimated its size around 240 BC. Columbus's critics doubted his much-too-small estimate of the distance, not the shape. The flat-earth story spread in the 1800s.

cards.title: Medieval people thought the Earth was flat

quiz.why: A transformer is the neural-network design, introduced in 2017, that lets a model weigh how every word relates to every other.

cards.title: What does the 'T' in GPT stand for?

quiz.q: The word 'robot' comes from a Czech word meaning...
quiz.why: It comes from 'robota', forced labour. Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. introduced it; his brother Josef suggested the word.

cards.title: Where does the word 'robot' come from?

quiz.q: Stretched end to end, the DNA in a single human cell would be about...
quiz.why: About 2 metres of DNA is wound around proteins and coiled tightly enough to fit inside a nucleus a few thousandths of a millimetre wide.

cards.title: How long is the DNA in one of your cells?

cards.body: That's an economists' estimate from Commerce Department data. Imports of capital goods, which include computer equipment, hit a record $158 billion.

stat.label: Rough share of the US trade deficit in September from computers, peripherals and semiconductors

cards.title: Computers and chips drove most of the US trade gap

cards.body: Quark-gluon plasma was long studied by colliding lead nuclei. New results show signs of it with oxygen and neon, which have a tiny fraction of lead's protons and neutrons.
cards.title: The LHC found Big Bang soup in much smaller smashes

cards.body: Japanese researchers found adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine and uracil in grains of asteroid Ryugu brought back by Hayabusa2. All five showed up in both samples tested, in similar amounts. That suggests life's genetic building blocks were common in the early Solar System.
cards.more:
Hayabusa2 returned 5.4 grams of Ryugu to Earth in 2020. Uracil had already been reported in 2023; this study, in Nature Astronomy, completes the set.
NASA's untouched Bennu samples also yielded all five in 2025. Pristine samples matter because meteorites that land on Earth can pick up contamination.
Different space rocks favour different bases, and ammonia may shift the balance. None of this means life existed on the asteroid, only that its ingredients did.
cards.title: All five letters of DNA and RNA turned up in asteroid dust

cards.body: Thermodynamics normally forbids a black hole from breaking apart. A theory paper from the University of Southern Denmark finds a narrow loophole for black holes spinning close to their maximum rate. Nobody has seen it happen, and the authors can't yet say how likely it is.
cards.more:
The rule comes from entropy: two smaller black holes would hold less total entropy than one big one, which the second law of thermodynamics doesn't allow.
Rapid rotation changes the bookkeeping, but the two pieces would also have to fly apart rather than merge again, which closes most of the window.
Some theories with extra dimensions make splitting easier, especially into one large and one tiny piece. The team suggests gamma-ray telescopes like Fermi could look for signals from such fragments. The study is in Physical Review D.
cards.title: A fast enough spin might let a black hole split in two

cards.body: Most metals turn brittle when deeply frozen. Oxford-led researchers tested two experimental niobium-titanium alloys at 20 kelvin and saw no measurable slide toward brittleness. Tiny mirror-image shifts in their crystal structure absorb the strain instead.
cards.more:
That temperature, -253°C, is roughly where hydrogen turns liquid, which matters for fuel tanks and cryogenic equipment.
The trick is called twinning: small zones of the crystal flip into a mirrored arrangement, creating fresh defects that let the metal deform instead of crack.
The tests used neutron beams at the UK's ISIS facility. These are lab-scale alloys; the authors point to energy, transport and aerospace as possible future uses. The work appears in Nature.
cards.title: Two new alloys stay tough at minus 253 degrees Celsius

cards.body: Fossil hunters at Wadi Moghra in northern Egypt found the lower jaw of a new ape, Masripithecus moghraensis, about 17 to 18 million years old. It is the first definite fossil ape from North Africa, and analyses place it closer to living apes than East African apes of its age.
cards.more:
The team from Mansoura University and the University of Southern California recovered the fossils in 2023 and 2024. Only the jaw is known, so its body size and behaviour remain a mystery.
Its teeth suggest it mostly ate fruit but could manage nuts or seeds.
The researchers estimate that the common ancestor of all living apes lived 23 to 16 million years ago, most likely in North Africa or the Middle East. They do not claim this species is that ancestor. The study is in Science.
cards.title: An 18-million-year-old ape jaw from Egypt points to North Africa

cards.body: A Neanderthal from Shanidar Cave in Iraqi Kurdistan, about 75,000 years old, has a round hole in the left shoulder blade. Cambridge researchers think a wooden spear entered the chest and passed out the back. Who threw it, and whether it was an accident, is unknown.
cards.more:
The individual, nicknamed Shanidar A, was about 45 at death. An earlier blow had split a tooth, but tartar buildup shows they lived at least a year afterwards, likely with help from others.
The body lay in a burial area with four other people, including an infant.
Wooden spears are old technology: examples from Schöningen, Germany, date to around 200,000 years ago. The study is in Scientific Reports.
cards.title: A Neanderthal shoulder blade bears a 15 mm hole from a spear

cards.body: Among nearly 486,000 adults followed for about nine years, regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower risk of vascular disease. Black tea showed the most consistent link; drinking it 'burning hot' was tied to higher risk. It's an association, not proof that tea protects the heart.
cards.more:
Among weekly tea drinkers, the lowest estimated risk came at roughly six to eight cups a day, and moderate-strength tea did better than strong.
The lowest risk overall combined tea drinking with not smoking and being physically active, which hints at how lifestyle factors cluster together.
The study, in the Journal of Internal Medicine, found no mechanism and did not define a harmful temperature.
cards.title: Tea drinkers in a huge Chinese study had fewer heart problems

cards.body: On healthy, protected reefs, University of Sydney researchers found coral survived nearly 75% of crown-of-thorns starfish feeding events. The patches they opened up regrew with different corals, possibly boosting diversity. Big outbreaks remain a serious threat.
cards.more:
The Great Barrier Reef has had four major outbreaks since the 1960s, roughly every 15 years, and they can strip whole reefs.
At low numbers, though, the starfish act like moderate disturbance. Fast-growing Acropora didn't take over the gaps; Montipora and Porites did instead.
The idea that middling disturbance keeps ecosystems diverse is called the intermediate disturbance hypothesis. The study is in Ecology and Evolution.
cards.title: The reef's notorious coral-eating starfish may also help it

cards.body: Frogs vanished at a Brazilian research station between 1979 and 1982. Testing over 370 preserved specimens, researchers found none collected before 1979 carried chytrid fungus, but more than half from the 1980s did. The fungus wasn't even named until 1999.
cards.more:
The team from the Smithsonian and Penn State used jars of specimens gathered decades ago, including by herpetologist W. Ronald Heyer.
Visits from 2022 to 2024 found 12 of the 17 species studied; five were missing. Most have recovered even though the fungus is still around.
Oddly, the species that declined most showed no detectable infection, so frogs may differ in how well they tolerate it. The study is in Molecular Ecology.
cards.title: Museum frogs solve a 1980s die-off in Brazil's Atlantic Forest

cards.body: A University of Georgia study followed more than 8,200 adults over 50 for 24 years. Higher body mass index was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking, most clearly in people over 65. The study shows a link, not that weight causes decline.
cards.more:
Each one-point rise in BMI went with a faster rate of cognitive decline in the data.
Possible explanations include inflammation, blood flow and insulin resistance, but the study didn't test them.
BMI is a blunt measure; the article notes that adding waist size changes estimates of how many people count as obese. The paper is in the Journal of Neurology.
cards.title: Higher BMI tracked faster memory decline over 24 years

cards.body: Thirty-one healthy adults aged 60 to 75 ate 60 grams of unsalted roasted peanuts a day for 16 weeks. MRI scans showed better insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain areas than in a peanut-free phase. It's a small, industry-funded study.
cards.more:
The Maastricht University trial was a crossover: each person did both the peanut and the peanut-free phases, so they served as their own comparison.
Regions that responded included the hippocampus, a key memory hub. Insulin helps brain cells use energy, so better response there is considered a healthy sign.
The Peanut Institute Foundation funded it, though the article says it had no role in the design or analysis. Bigger trials are needed. Published in Food & Function.
cards.title: Daily peanuts improved brain insulin response in a small trial

cards.body: Fastagger, a three-person Kenyan company, makes AI models that work without internet on low-power phones. Its assistant Auni is built into M-Pesa's business app, and the company says about 6,000 businesses have signed up.
cards.more:
Mobile money is everywhere in Kenya: the article cites a survey showing over 80% of adults use it.
Fastagger also makes an SMS-based tool for managing security guards, a big workforce in Kenya. It has been through accelerator programs run by Google, Microsoft and NVIDIA.
One economist quoted worries AI could split businesses into those that get good tools and those that don't, which is the gap offline models aim to close.
cards.title: A Kenyan startup builds AI that runs offline on cheap phones

cards.body: A researcher auditing the PHP language with help from AI tools found a way to run arbitrary code on sites using WordPress or Drupal. It was reported and patched before attackers got it, as far as anyone knows. Experts say AI is speeding up bug hunting for both sides.
cards.more:
The bug, dubbed PHP2Shell, grew from an out-of-memory error reported to the PHP Foundation as early as 2024.
The audit was by Calif, sponsored by OpenAI; the article says it took the researcher about two weeks to turn the bug into an exploit, and four engineers two months to build the fix.
IEEE Spectrum frames it as AI forcing the industry to pay off decades of old code, or 'technical debt'.
cards.title: AI helped find a PHP flaw that exposed huge numbers of websites

cards.body: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate from 4.60% to 4.85%, its fifth rise this year and the highest since 2008. Six board members voted for the hike and three to hold. It now expects inflation to stay above 3% until late 2027.
cards.more:
That's about three quarters later than the bank previously forecast.
Governor Michele Bullock said the bank isn't trying to push the economy into recession, though growth is slowing markedly. It sees unemployment edging up to 5.1% by late 2028, from 4.7% now.
Some economists expect another hike early next year.
cards.title: Australia's central bank lifted rates to an 18-year high

cards.body: On November 18 a radio signal will take a full day to reach Voyager 1, so a command and its reply take 48 hours. NASA nearly lost contact in October when a set of thrusters failed and backups kicked in.
cards.more:
Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is moving at about 61,000 km/h through interstellar space.
Each Voyager loses about 4 watts of power a year. In September engineers swapped three devices for lower-power versions, an operation nicknamed the 'Big Bang', to keep instruments running longer.
Contact dropped on October 18 and returned on October 20. NASA hasn't yet found why the thrusters stopped.

stat.label: Voyager 1's distance on Nov 18, 2026: one light-day

cards.title: Voyager 1 is about to be one light-day from Earth

cards.body: Australia plans about 14,000 chargers on power poles from 2027. In Sydney's eastern suburbs, chargers with a dedicated bay get used far more than those where any car can park.
cards.more:
Figures are charging sessions in one year at three chargers in the Waverley, Woollahra and Randwick council areas.
A council program manager expects most of the new pole chargers to lack dedicated parking. One industry analyst argues official modelling overstates how many EVs each charger will serve.
cards.title: Kerbside EV chargers sit idle without their own parking spot

beats: Entropy roughly counts how many ways a system's insides could be arranged.
The second law says the total entropy of an isolated system never goes down.
A black hole's entropy grows with the area of its event horizon, which scales with mass squared.
Split one into two equal halves and the total area, and entropy, drops by half.
So splitting breaks the second law, unless something like extreme spin changes the bookkeeping.
cards.more:
This link between horizon area and entropy comes from Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking in the 1970s.
It's also why black holes merge so readily: one big hole has more entropy than two small ones.
cards.title: Why a black hole can't simply snap in half

beats: A gravity assist sends a probe close past a moving planet.
From the planet's view, the probe leaves as fast as it arrived, just bent in a new direction.
But the planet is racing around the Sun, and the probe gets dragged along with it.
Seen from the Sun, the probe gains speed while the planet slows by an unmeasurably tiny amount.
Voyager 1 used Jupiter and Saturn this way to reach the edge of the Solar System.
cards.more:
The same trick can slow a probe down by passing in front of a planet instead of behind it.
Voyager 2 chained flybys of all four giant planets, a lineup that happens roughly once every 175 years.
cards.title: How spacecraft steal speed from planets

beats: DNA uses four bases: A, T, G and C. RNA swaps T for U.
Cells read the sequence in three-letter words called codons.
Four letters in triplets give 64 codons, enough for 20 amino acids plus stop signals.
Each gene's codons line up amino acids into a chain that folds into a protein.
Proteins do most of the work of life, from digesting food to building muscle.
cards.more:
Several codons often mean the same amino acid, so some typos in DNA change nothing.
Finding all five bases in asteroid samples shows the letters can form without life; the code that uses them is a separate puzzle.
cards.title: How four chemical letters spell out a living thing

beats: An AI model is mostly a huge list of numbers called weights.
Each weight is often stored with 16 bits of precision.
Quantization rounds weights to 8 or even 4 bits, shrinking the model two to four times.
Smaller weights mean less memory and power, so models can run without the cloud.
The cost is a little accuracy, which careful rounding keeps small.
cards.more:
Developers often pair quantization with smaller models trained for one job, rather than shrinking a giant general model.
Running on the device also keeps data private and works where internet is patchy.
cards.title: How a big AI model squeezes onto a cheap phone

beats: A bond's yield is the yearly return you get for lending money.
The yield curve plots yields for loans of different lengths, from months to decades.
Normally longer loans pay more, as a reward for tying money up longer.
When short-term yields rise above long-term ones, the curve is called inverted.
In the US, inversions have come before many recessions, though the signal isn't perfect.
cards.more:
An inversion often means markets expect interest rates to fall later, usually because they expect the economy to weaken.
Central bank hikes push short-term yields up directly, which is one way curves invert.
cards.title: Why investors watch the yield curve

beats: The mean adds everything up and divides by the count.
The median is simply the middle value when you line them up.
Put nine people earning 50,000 in a room with a billionaire.
The mean income jumps to about 100 million; the median stays at 50,000.
For skewed things like income or house prices, the median usually tells the truer story.
cards.more:
That's why statistics agencies usually report median household income.
A mean far above the median is itself a clue that a few huge values are pulling it up.
cards.title: When the average lies: mean versus median

beats: An unreliable narrator tells the story in a way we can't fully believe.
Critic Wayne Booth named the idea in 1961.
The narrator may lie, misunderstand, or be blinded by pride or madness.
In Poe's 'The Tell-Tale Heart', the narrator's claims of sanity are the giveaway.
The fun is reading between the lines to find the story they won't tell.
cards.more:
Writers signal unreliability through contradictions, other characters' reactions, or details the narrator mentions without understanding.
A child narrator can be unreliable without lying at all, simply by not grasping what they see.
cards.title: The unreliable narrator, and why we trust them anyway

myth.claim: Bats are blind and find their way only by sound.
myth.truth: No bat species is blind. Many fruit bats see well and don't echolocate at all. Bats that do echolocate still use their eyes too, for example to navigate over longer distances.

cards.title: Blind as a bat

myth.claim: Viking warriors wore helmets with horns.
myth.truth: No evidence shows it. The one nearly complete Viking-age helmet, found at Gjermundbu in Norway, has no horns. The image largely comes from 19th-century art and costumes, notably for Wagner's opera cycle The Ring.

cards.title: Horned Viking helmets

myth.claim: Ending a sentence with a preposition is a grammar error.
myth.truth: It's a myth borrowed from Latin, where it's impossible. The poet John Dryden criticised it in 1672 and the idea stuck. English has always done it: 'What are you looking at?' is perfectly correct.

cards.title: Never end a sentence with a preposition

quiz.q: How many people need to be in a room for a better-than-even chance that two share a birthday?
quiz.why: With 23 people there are 253 possible pairs, and each pair is a chance for a match. The odds pass 50%. With 57 people they top 99%.

cards.title: The birthday surprise

quiz.q: Did Cleopatra live closer in time to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza or to the Moon landing?
quiz.why: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BC, about 2,500 years before Cleopatra. She died in 30 BC, just under 2,000 years before 1969.

cards.title: Cleopatra's place in time

quiz.q: Roughly what share of all water on Earth is fresh water?
quiz.why: Almost all of it is salty ocean. And most fresh water is locked in ice caps, glaciers and underground, so lakes and rivers hold only a tiny sliver.

cards.title: How much of Earth's water is fresh?

cards.body: Combining Hubble's visible light with Webb's infrared, astronomers spotted 27 previously unknown trans-Neptunian objects, the smallest just 5 km wide. Calm 'cold' objects and ones flung outward by migrating planets look surprisingly alike.
cards.more:
Trans-Neptunian objects are leftover building blocks from the Solar System's birth, orbiting out past Neptune.
'Cold' ones stay near the flat plane of the planets; 'hot' ones were scattered onto tilted paths as the giant planets shifted. Their similar surface colours suggest collisions changed them less than expected.
Webb also found fewer very small objects than some planet-formation models predict, a clue for how these bodies first clumped together.
cards.title: Hubble and Webb found 27 new icy worlds beyond Neptune

cards.body: A classic 1969 model says interstellar gas settles into a cold or a warm state. A new 3D map of our galactic neighbourhood suggests 41% sits in an unstable in-between state instead. The paper is still under peer review.
cards.more:
Technion undergraduate Jonathan Shelest and professor Shmuel Bialy combined a 3D dust map with a radiation map, about 200 gigabytes of data.
They found roughly 27% of nearby gas cold (around 100 kelvins), 32% warm (around 8,000 kelvins) and 41% in between.
If that holds, gas constantly heating and cooling might help explain why stars form more slowly than expected. Outside astronomers are urging caution until the work is checked.
cards.title: The gas between stars may be far more restless than we thought

cards.body: Physicists at Southampton and IIT Kanpur propose that a weakly interacting heavy neutrino briefly dominated the young universe, nudging the balance between matter and antimatter. It is theory for now, but it could leave traces in primordial gravitational waves.
cards.more:
The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter, which would have annihilated each other. Something tipped the scales.
In this model, the heavy neutrino's long life creates a short matter-dominated era. That shifts the temperature at which particles like electrons interacted with their antiparticles via the Higgs field.
The paper appears in Physical Review Letters. Future gravitational-wave detectors could, in principle, test it.
cards.title: A long-lived heavy neutrino might explain why matter survived

cards.body: The 1989 cold-fusion claim was never replicated. A quieter field swaps electrons for muons, 207 times heavier, which squeeze atoms small enough to fuse. A Japanese team recently made the first direct X-ray measurement of muonic hydrogen molecules.
cards.more:
This is from an essay by George Musser looking back at cold fusion and what grew from it.
A muon can catalyse fusion again and again, but it would need roughly 300 or more cycles to pay back the energy of making it. Most physicists doubt that's reachable.
Still, exotic atoms like these are useful labs for testing physics in extreme electric fields.
cards.title: Cold fusion flopped, but heavy-electron fusion research lives on

cards.body: For IEEE Spectrum, Benjamin Skuse generated papers with chatbots and an automated research system. Integrity checks caught a dozen invented references in the first attempt; the second, made in about two hours, had none. Neither paper was accepted.
cards.more:
Round one used free versions of ChatGPT and Gemini. Screening tools flagged 12 'ghost' references that point to papers that don't exist.
Round two used a system called FARS, which drafted a proposal in 21 minutes, ran an experiment overnight and wrote the paper. Its references were real, though it leaned heavily on unreviewed preprints.
The piece cites an estimate that 57% of 2025 papers showed detectable signs of language-model help, up from 12% in 2023.
cards.title: A writer used AI to fake a research paper, then tried to submit it

cards.body: UMass Amherst researchers grew lab heart cells around a 7-by-8 mm mesh of 64 tiny piezoelectric strips that make electricity when flexed. The team reports about ten times the energy density of earlier designs, a step toward self-powered implants.
cards.more:
Piezoelectric materials produce a voltage when squeezed or bent. Here, each strip moves with the beating tissue.
Over 15 days, stem-cell-derived heart cells grew into a continuous sheet around the mesh.
Outside experts flag open questions: whether it lasts for years, scar tissue forming around it, and the strips being made of a lead-based ceramic.
cards.title: A mesh woven into heart tissue turns heartbeats into power

cards.body: French startup HyLight flies 12-metre autonomous airships powered by fuel cells to check grid and rail lines. It says they stay up to 10 hours and cost about 50 times less to run than helicopters. Those figures are company claims.
cards.more:
Helicopters are the traditional way to inspect long stretches of power lines; drones are cheaper but have short battery life.
HyLight says it has logged more than 750 flight hours and has permission to fly beyond the pilot's line of sight. French grid operator Enedis and rail network SNCF Réseau are customers.
The company raised €13 million and plans to fly 15 airships at once in 2027.
cards.title: Hydrogen blimps are being sent to inspect power lines

cards.body: In a trial of 96 adults aged 18 to 45 with early type 2 diabetes and obesity, 54% on a supervised 800–900 calorie plan plus exercise reached remission in 24 weeks, versus about 4% with usual care.
cards.more:
Remission here means blood sugar back below the diabetes range without glucose-lowering medicine.
The intervention group lost 8.4 kg on average, compared with 1.2 kg in usual care. Side effects were more common in the intensive group, which is why it was medically supervised.
The RESET for Remission trial ran in England and Canada and was published in The Lancet Regional Health – Americas.
cards.title: An intensive diet put half of young adults' diabetes into remission

cards.body: McGill researchers tested 12 diets in mice and found some linked to obesity made immune-checkpoint drugs work better, helped by gut bacteria. The team stresses this is mice only and patients should not change diets on its basis.
cards.more:
Doctors have noticed an 'obesity paradox': in some cancers, people with obesity respond better to immunotherapy. Nobody knows why.
This study, published in Nature, points to diet and gut microbes acting together, even over short periods.
It is a clue for future research, not a treatment recommendation.
cards.title: Some 'unhealthy' diets boosted cancer immunotherapy in mice

cards.body: A UCLA study of about 1,650 Californians found long-term residential exposure to chlorpyrifos linked to more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's. It shows an association, not proof of cause, though mouse and zebrafish tests point to a mechanism.
cards.more:
Researchers matched people's home address histories to state pesticide-spraying records, comparing 829 people with Parkinson's to 824 without.
Mice exposed to the pesticide lost dopamine-producing neurons and developed movement problems. In zebrafish, the damage was tied to a disrupted cellular clean-up process called autophagy.
The study is in Molecular Neurodegeneration.
cards.title: Living near a common pesticide is linked to higher Parkinson's risk

cards.body: Pooling six studies of 2,684 older adults without memory problems, researchers found very high blood levels of a protein called p-tau217 were linked to a much higher chance of cognitive impairment within 5 to 10 years.
cards.more:
Among people with the highest levels, the estimated chance of impairment was 38% within five years. Ten-year estimates were higher but rest on much less data.
The link held even after accounting for amyloid plaques and the APOE4 gene variant.
The researchers say such blood tests are not yet recommended for routine screening of people without symptoms. Published in JAMA.
cards.title: A blood marker tracked Alzheimer's risk up to a decade ahead

cards.body: NASA Landsat images of Vega Island in the Weddell Sea look like a grinning skull. A glaciologist says an unusually warm 2026 winter left little fresh snow, exposing dark ice that soaks up more sunlight and may melt faster.
cards.more:
The images compare March 22, 2025 with October 10, 2026.
Fresh snow is bright and reflects sunlight; older glacier ice is darker and absorbs more. That feedback can speed up melting once snow cover is lost.
A 1982 study counted 29 glaciers on the island, and one of them, Devil's Bay Glacier, has been losing mass since monitoring began in the late 1990s.
cards.title: A skull-shaped island in Antarctica shows its bare ice

cards.body: Hair and nail tests on eight freeze-dried Inca mummies from Andean mountain shrines found coca in all eight and alcohol in four. The 500-year-old rituals, called capacocha, varied more than historians assumed.
cards.more:
Hair grows slowly, so it keeps a timeline of what a person consumed over months.
The study, in the journal Antiquity, also found harmine, a compound from a psychoactive vine, in the mummy known as the Lady of Ampato.
Lead author Dagmara Socha of the University of Warsaw says the findings show the ceremony was not one standard script.
cards.title: Inca mummies reveal what the children consumed before sacrifice

cards.body: Seven metres under an old riverbed in Beijing's Fengtai district, archaeologists uncovered three wooden boats up to 15 metres long. They are the largest inland vessels of their era found in North China, and one bears ten 'official' characters.
cards.more:
Radiocarbon dating places them in the late Eastern Han to Wei and Jin periods, about 1,800 years ago.
The character 官 (guan, meaning 'official') painted on the best-preserved boat hints it served the state, perhaps hauling goods along canals.
The boats were excavated in late 2025; researchers presented updated findings on October 31.
cards.title: Three 1,800-year-old riverboats were found beneath Beijing

cards.body: Slovak central bank chief Peter Kazimir said the European Central Bank will have to raise rates again to stop high inflation becoming entrenched. The ECB held rates last week; markets expect two to three hikes over the next year.
cards.more:
When inflation lingers, people and firms start expecting it and build it into wages and prices. Central bankers call that 'entrenched' inflation, and it is harder to undo.
Kazimir also noted growth is holding up partly because government budgets are supporting the economy, which can work against a central bank trying to cool demand.
cards.title: An ECB official says Europe will need more rate hikes

beats: Atomic nuclei are positively charged, so they push each other away fiercely.
To fuse, two nuclei must get close enough for the strong force to grab them.
Stars manage it with crushing gravity and temperatures of millions of degrees.
Swap an atom's electron for a muon, 207 times heavier, and the atom shrinks dramatically.
Nuclei sit so close they can fuse cold, but each muon decays in about two millionths of a second.
cards.title: Why fusion needs millions of degrees, and how muons cheat

beats: Albedo is how much sunlight a surface reflects instead of absorbing.
Fresh snow reflects most incoming sunlight, so it stays cool.
Old ice and bare rock are darker and absorb more of that energy as heat.
More heat melts more snow, exposing more dark surface underneath.
That loop, called the ice-albedo feedback, helps explain why polar regions warm fastest.
cards.title: Why dark ice melts faster than snow

beats: A central bank sets the rate at which banks borrow short-term money.
Raise it, and loans, mortgages and credit cards get more expensive for everyone.
People and businesses borrow and spend less, so demand for goods cools.
With fewer buyers chasing products, sellers raise prices more slowly.
The effect takes months to show up, and the cost is usually slower growth.
cards.title: How raising interest rates slows inflation

beats: A language model learns what text usually looks like, not a list of verified facts.
A citation has a familiar shape: authors, a title, a journal, a year.
The model can produce that shape fluently even when no such paper exists.
Tools that look up real databases before answering cut this error sharply.
So check every AI-supplied reference by finding the paper itself.
cards.title: Why chatbots invent references that don't exist

beats: Relative risk compares two groups: exposed versus not exposed.
Absolute risk is the actual chance something happens to a person.
Imagine a 1-in-1,000 baseline; 2.5 times higher makes it 2.5 in 1,000.
The same multiplier on a 1-in-10 baseline would mean 25 in 100.
Always ask for the baseline, and whether the link is proven cause or correlation.
cards.title: '2.5 times the risk' depends on the starting risk

beats: 'In medias res' is Latin for 'into the middle of things.'
The Roman poet Horace praised Homer for opening stories mid-action.
The Odyssey begins with Odysseus stranded, years into his journey home.
The backstory arrives later through flashbacks and characters' retellings.
Dropping readers into action creates questions, and questions keep people reading.
cards.title: In medias res: why great stories start in the middle

myth.claim: People learn best when teaching matches their style: visual, auditory or hands-on.
myth.truth: People do have preferences, but controlled studies haven't found that matching lessons to a preferred style improves learning. What helps is matching the method to the material, like diagrams for maps, plus practice testing and spacing out study.

cards.title: Learning styles

myth.claim: Blood without oxygen is blue, which is why veins look blue.
myth.truth: Human blood is always red: bright red with oxygen, darker red without. Veins look blue because of how skin and tissue absorb and scatter light before it reaches your eyes.

cards.title: Blue blood in your veins

myth.claim: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
myth.truth: Tall, pointed, exposed objects get hit again and again. New York's Empire State Building is struck roughly 20 to 25 times a year on average.

cards.title: Lightning never strikes twice

quiz.q: The word 'quarantine' comes from an Italian phrase meaning…
quiz.why: Venetian 'quaranta giorni' meant forty days, the time ships from plague-hit ports waited before landing in the 1300s–1400s.

cards.title: Where does 'quarantine' come from?

quiz.q: The Inca Empire had no known writing system. What did it use to record numbers and data?
quiz.why: Quipus were bundles of coloured, knotted strings; the knot type and position encoded numbers for taxes, censuses and storehouses.

cards.title: How did the Inca keep records?

quiz.q: You pick one of 3 doors; one hides a car. The host, who knows, opens another door showing a goat. Switch or stay?
quiz.why: Your first pick wins 1/3 of the time. The host's reveal concentrates the remaining 2/3 onto the other closed door.

cards.title: The Monty Hall problem

cards.body: Same charge, far more mass. That extra weight pulls a muonic atom much tighter, which is why muons can coax hydrogen nuclei close enough to fuse.

stat.label: a muon's mass compared to an electron's

cards.title: The electron's heavy cousin

cards.body: Fuel, transport and food costs are pushing prices up. Economists polled by The Manila Times expect October inflation near 7.7%; official data lands November 5.
cards.title: Philippine inflation has climbed fast in a year

cards.body: OpenAI says its models proved that every nontrivial zero of the zeta function sits inside a strip narrower than the classic 0-to-1 band. The tighter version puts them between 1/12 and 11/12. Most experts think it holds up; some want humans to check every line first.
cards.more:
The Riemann hypothesis says all the nontrivial zeros sit exactly on the line where the real part is 1/2. Proving they stay any fixed distance away from the edges of the 0-to-1 strip is called the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, and nobody had managed it.
A first, 199-page version (zeros between 1/8 and 7/8) was machine-checked in the proof language Lean. A later 49-page version tightened the band to 1/12 and 11/12; it is the one mathematicians are scrutinising, and it has not yet been formally verified.
The novelty is in combining existing number-theory tools in a new way. Peter Sarnak says he won't call it a theorem until humans have checked it, and Will Sawin doubts it brings the full hypothesis much closer.
cards.title: An AI proved a weaker cousin of the Riemann hypothesis

cards.body: The brown dwarf SIMP 0136 cycles through three recurring weather states as it spins. Temperature shifts and how its clouds are stacked drive most of the change, found a Trinity College Dublin team using Webb data.
cards.more:
A brown dwarf is too heavy to be a planet and too light to fuse hydrogen like a star. That makes it a useful stand-in for giant exoplanets, which are harder to observe.
The team used a statistical technique called principal component analysis to pull the main patterns out of Webb's spectra. It is a quick way to find which atmospheric processes matter before running expensive models.
cards.title: Webb mapped the weather on a failed star 20 light-years away

cards.body: Around 21 young stars, unusually warm and flickering dust looks like debris from planet-scale crashes. About a third of the disks are silica-rich, a sign of violent impacts between Mars-sized bodies.
cards.more:
Silica-rich disks only showed up around stars younger than 300 million years, the age range when rocky planets are still being assembled. The rest look like gentler, grazing hits between Moon-sized objects.
Our own Moon most likely formed from this kind of collision, when a Mars-sized body struck the early Earth.
cards.title: Webb caught the dust of Mars-sized worlds colliding

cards.body: After stripping out El Niño, volcanoes and solar cycles, a Potsdam Institute study finds the last decade warmed at about 0.35°C per decade.
cards.more: The study, by Stefan Rahmstorf and Grant Foster in Geophysical Research Letters, does not pin down why the rate jumped, though the result matches what climate models expect. How fast warming continues depends on how quickly fossil-fuel CO2 emissions fall.
cards.title: Warming has nearly doubled its pace

cards.body: In 87,577 adults who wore light sensors for about eight years, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight a day predicted dementia more strongly than six well-known risk factors. It's a correlation, not proof that light protects the brain.
cards.more:
Averaging more than 1,000 lux during the day was linked to a 16% lower dementia risk. For scale: a well-lit office is around 300–500 lux, an overcast sky outdoors is usually several thousand, and direct sun can top 100,000. Light at night showed no meaningful link.
The study was led by researchers at Guangzhou Medical University and published in General Psychiatry.
cards.title: Daylight and dementia

cards.body: McGill researchers found T cells sense the firmness of their surroundings. Stiffer tissue nudges them to become long-lived memory cells that stay put and guard that spot.
cards.more:
In collagen gels of different stiffness, human and mouse T cells in firmer gels were more likely to take on 'tissue-resident memory' traits. The team now wants to find the molecular sensor that detects the force.
It matters because tumours are often dense and stiff, and cancer immunotherapies need T cells that can get in and stay. The work appeared in Nature Immunology.
cards.title: Immune cells can feel how stiff your tissue is

cards.body: An updated global estimate puts snakebite deaths at 274,000 to 513,000 a year. Sub-Saharan Africa carries about 45% of the cases and deaths.
cards.more: The estimate, drawing on data from 79 countries, updates a 2008 global study by the same group at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine. Most victims are rural farm workers far from antivenom.
cards.title: Snakebites are a far bigger killer than we thought

cards.body: The 'Ubeidiya site south of the Sea of Galilee is at least 1.9 million years old, not 1.2–1.6 million. That makes it as old as Dmanisi in Georgia, among the earliest known settlements outside Africa.
cards.more: The redating suggests groups carrying two different stone-tool traditions, the simpler Oldowan and the more shaped Acheulean, spread out of Africa at roughly the same time rather than in neat successive waves.
cards.title: Humans left Africa earlier than this site's old date said

cards.body: Fortifications at Oued Beht, dated to roughly 4,000–3,500 years ago, are likely the earliest confirmed defensive construction in North Africa outside the Nile Valley.
cards.more: The earthworks were first noticed in the 1930s, but excavations since 2023 revealed their ditch, rampart and wall phases. The settlement covers at least ten hectares, which points to societies in the Maghreb that were more organised than historians had assumed.
cards.title: A 4,000-year-old wall in Morocco rewrites North Africa's past

cards.body: Galaxies with the fastest supernova winds let the least ionizing light escape. That cuts against the popular idea that such winds cleared the paths that ended the universe's early hydrogen fog.
cards.more:
For a few hundred million years after the Big Bang, space was filled with neutral hydrogen that absorbed ultraviolet light. Starlight eventually stripped those atoms of electrons, a process called reionization, and the universe became transparent.
The new Hubble work, studying nearby starburst galaxies as stand-ins, finds the winds spread gas and dust that block radiation instead. The authors suggest light from young massive stars may escape before supernovae begin.
cards.title: Hubble upends a theory of how the early universe got clear

cards.body: A spiral molecule spins when electrons flow through it, and reversing the voltage reverses the spin. The spinning even makes it conduct better.
cards.more: Built by a team led by the University of Augsburg with the Weizmann Institute and others, and published in Nature. Possible uses include molecular electronics, spintronics, and pumps for microscopic volumes of fluid.
cards.title: An Archimedes screw the size of one molecule

cards.body: Startup NVision reports in Nature an organic molecule that stores quantum information in its spin and talks to light. Because it can be laid down as a thin film, it might be made in existing chip foundries.
cards.more:
The company says the design tolerates up to 70% photon loss, which would let it work with standard silicon photonics, and it plans a first prototype chip in late 2026. These are the company's claims; scaling is the hard part every qubit type still faces.
Why molecules? Most qubits today are superconducting circuits or trapped atoms that need elaborate custom hardware. A qubit that rides on ordinary manufacturing would change the economics.
cards.title: A qubit you could print onto a chip

cards.body: Trees sense their own shape and pull curved trunks upright with tension wood. New work shows it can form on both sides of a stem, working like opposing muscles.
cards.more: Scientists thought tension wood only formed on the upper side of a leaning stem, pulling it up. The INRAE team found a counter-pull on the opposite side that stops the stem overshooting and brings it back to nearly straight. The finding could help breed straighter timber and cereal crops that topple less. Published in New Phytologist.
cards.title: Trees have 'muscles' to straighten themselves

cards.body: A UCL study suggests their love of warm climates kept them in tropical refuges that stayed habitable after the asteroid hit. Small size, semi-aquatic habits and low energy needs helped too.
cards.more: Simulations showed equatorial regions stayed warm enough for crocodile relatives after the impact, unless sunlight dropped by as much as 15%, which would have made even those areas too cold. Published in Science Advances.
cards.title: Why crocodiles outlived the dinosaurs

cards.body: Intel fell about 30% on weak PC demand and heavy factory spending. Amazon reported a $42.4 billion free-cash-flow deficit over the past year, mostly from AI data centres, and the Nasdaq 100 was on track to lose over $1 trillion in a day.
cards.more:
Free cash flow is the cash a business generates from operations minus what it spends on capital investment like buildings, servers and chips. A company can be very profitable on paper and still burn cash if it is building fast.
That is the market's worry: the big platforms are spending enormous sums on AI infrastructure now, and investors are asking when it pays back.
cards.title: AI spending spooked tech stocks on Friday

cards.body: Alongside a multi-gigawatt Nvidia deal, Oracle Cloud will offer Google's TPUs for the first time, plus inference chips from Cerebras and SambaNova.
cards.more:
GPUs started as graphics chips and are flexible enough to run almost any AI workload. TPUs are Google's custom chips built specifically for the matrix maths in neural networks. Inference chips are tuned for running trained models cheaply rather than training them.
A cloud offering all three is a sign that buyers want alternatives to Nvidia, whether for price or supply.
cards.title: Oracle's cloud will rent out Google's AI chips

beats: Your text is chopped into tokens, pieces averaging about three-quarters of a word.
Each token becomes a long list of numbers that encodes its meaning.
Attention layers let every token look at every other one to work out context.
The model outputs a probability for every possible next token.
It picks one, adds it to the text, and runs the whole thing again.
cards.more: That loop is why models write one token at a time, and why longer answers take longer. 'Temperature' controls how adventurous the pick in step four is: low means it almost always takes the most likely token, high means it samples more widely.
cards.title: How a language model writes a sentence

beats: Rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly return to get the years it takes to double.
At 8% a year, money doubles roughly every 9 years.
1,000 becomes 2,000 after 9 years, then 4,000 after 18.
After 27 years it's 8,000; after 36, about 16,000.
The last 9 years add more than the first 27 combined.
cards.more: The rule of 72 is an approximation that works best for rates between about 6% and 10%. The same maths works against you on debt, and inflation compounds too: at 6% inflation, prices double in about 12 years.
cards.title: Why compounding feels slow, then sudden

beats: GPS satellites carry atomic clocks; your position comes from comparing their timestamps.
Weaker gravity up there makes their clocks run fast by about 45 microseconds a day.
Their speed makes them run slow by about 7 microseconds a day.
Net: about 38 microseconds a day ahead of clocks on the ground.
Light travels about 300 m per microsecond, so uncorrected you'd drift ~11 km a day.
cards.more: The first effect comes from general relativity (gravity slows time), the second from special relativity (motion slows time). Engineers set the satellite clocks slightly slow before launch so they tick at the right rate once in orbit.
cards.title: Your phone's GPS needs Einstein

beats: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4° relative to its orbit.
For half the year your hemisphere leans toward the Sun.
Sunlight then hits more directly and days run longer, so it's summer.
