Six months later you lean away: low sun, short days, winter.
Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.
cards.more: That's why the hemispheres have opposite seasons at the same moment. Near the equator the tilt matters less, so seasons there are defined more by rain than by temperature.
cards.title: Seasons aren't about distance from the Sun

beats: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. The test catches it 99% of the time and falsely flags 1% of healthy people.
Test 1,000 people: about 1 sick person tests positive.
Of the 999 healthy people, about 10 also test positive.
So of roughly 11 positives, only 1 is actually sick.
A positive result means about a 9% chance you have it. That's Bayes' theorem.
cards.more: The key is the base rate: how common the thing is before any test. When it's rare, false positives from the large healthy group swamp the true ones. Doctors handle this by retesting or testing only people with symptoms, which raises the base rate.
cards.title: A 99% accurate test can still mostly be wrong

beats: New experiences are first held by the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain.
During sleep, the hippocampus replays the day's patterns.
Replay gradually strengthens links in the cortex, where long-term memories live.
Each time you recall a memory, it becomes briefly editable, then is saved again.
That's why testing yourself beats rereading: retrieval itself strengthens the memory.
cards.more: The 'testing effect' is one of the most reliable findings in learning research. Spacing the practice out over days helps even more than cramming the same amount into one sitting.
cards.title: How a memory gets saved

beats: Chekhov's principle: if a gun hangs on the wall in act one, it should go off by act three.
Every vivid detail makes a promise to the reader.
Planting it early and paying it off later is called setup and payoff.
A red herring breaks the promise on purpose, to mislead.
Good mysteries use both, and play fair: the real clue was on the page all along.
cards.more: Chekhov made the point in letters to other writers, in a few different wordings. The broader lesson is economy: cut what doesn't earn its place, or make it earn it later.
cards.title: Chekhov's gun, and its trickster twin

beats: It's how far light travels in one year: about 9.46 trillion km.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach you.
Light from the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, takes about 4.2 years.
Looking far away means looking back in time.
cards.more: When Webb observed the brown dwarf SIMP 0136, 20 light-years away, the light it caught left there about 20 years ago. For the most distant galaxies, it's more than 13 billion years.
cards.title: A light-year measures distance, not time

myth.claim: We only use 10% of our brains.
myth.truth: Brain imaging shows activity in virtually every region over the course of a day, and damage to almost any small area causes some loss of function. The brain is about 2% of body weight but uses roughly 20% of its energy; evolution doesn't keep an expensive organ 90% idle.

cards.title: The 10% brain

myth.claim: The Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye.
myth.truth: It's long but only a few metres wide and close in colour to the land around it. Astronauts in low orbit generally report they can't pick it out unaided, and from the Moon no human structure is visible at all. City lights at night are much easier to spot.

cards.title: The Great Wall from space

myth.claim: Cracking your knuckles gives you arthritis.
myth.truth: The pop is a gas bubble forming in the joint fluid as the joint is pulled apart. Studies comparing habitual crackers with non-crackers haven't found higher arthritis rates. One doctor cracked only his left hand for about 60 years and found no difference between his hands.

cards.title: Knuckle cracking

quiz.q: Roughly how much of the universe's total matter and energy is ordinary matter: atoms, stars, planets, us?
quiz.why: About 5%. Dark matter is roughly 27% and dark energy roughly 68%. Everything we can see or touch is the small remainder.

cards.title: What's the universe made of?

quiz.q: When 'nice' entered English in the 1300s, what did it mean?
quiz.why: It came via Old French from Latin nescius, 'not knowing'. Over centuries it drifted through 'shy', 'fussy' and 'precise' before settling on 'pleasant' in the 1700s.

cards.title: The surprising history of 'nice'

quiz.why: Teaching at Oxford was underway by 1096. The Aztec Triple Alliance formed in 1428, and Tenochtitlan itself was founded around 1325.

cards.title: Which came first?
